rule: PASS iff (a) >= 3 of the proposed hypotheses have an executable implementation, (b) mean AST similarity within a hypothesis exceeds the mean between hypotheses with one-sided permutation p <= 0.05, (c) mean between-hypothesis AST similarity is lower than the mean pairwise similarity of the control group (plain independent generations), (d) the usable programs receive different scores on >= 50% of the calibration instances.

hypotheses.name: Deterministic rule cascade
hypotheses.mechanism: A fixed sequence of greedy rewrite passes infers the document style by voting, rebuilds rows from line fragments, normalizes each field with rules keyed to its position, then patches each row once using check-digit and arithmetic tests.
hypotheses.principle: The passes run in order. (1) Infer the separator, decimal mark, thousands style, pcs style and column order from the COLUMNS line and from majority votes over the body. (2) Drop lines that match no expected pattern, join wrapped fragments until four fields exist, and split merged lines into groups of four. (3) Map look-alike characters to letters or digits depending on the field slot. (4) Repair a code that fails its check digit by trying single-character edits. (5) Repair the arithmetic by recomputing whichever of QTY, UNIT or AMOUNT is inconsistent from the other two. Most values are intact, so a cheap greedy cascade should already recover nearly every field on clean, lookalike and broken_layout documents.
assumptions: Style features (separator, decimal mark, grouping, pcs) are recoverable by majority vote
At most one field per row is damaged in most rows, so the other two fields fix it arithmetically
Look-alike substitutions can be undone from context alone: letters cannot appear in digit slots and vice versa
hypotheses.resources: Linear in document length with tiny constants; well under 10 ms per document.
constraints: Cannot resolve rows where two or more of QTY/UNIT/AMOUNT are damaged by digit misreads
A wrong merge or wrap decision early in the cascade is never revisited
advantages: Very fast and robust against timeouts
Strong on look-alike confusions, which are fully reversible
weaknesses: Greedy: makes no use of subtotal or total redundancy to settle ambiguous rows
Lost or doubled digits in two fields of the same row give a wrong UNIT
A misread code may have several single-edit candidates that pass the check digit; the cascade picks one arbitrarily
hypotheses.test: Measure field accuracy per family against a synthetic generator built from the spec. The hypothesis is wrong if accuracy on misread or lost_chars falls more than ~10 points below a candidate-lattice method, or if layout reconstruction fails on more than a few percent of broken_layout rows.

hypotheses.name: Per-row noisy-channel candidate lattice
hypotheses.mechanism: For each reconstructed row, enumerate weighted inverse-channel candidates per field, then pick the joint (code, qty, unit, amount) tuple that maximizes channel likelihood subject to the check digit and qty*unit == amount.
hypotheses.principle: Model every degradation operation with a cost: look-alike swap, each listed digit misread, lost digit, doubled digit, lost decimal mark. For each observed field token, generate original strings reachable within one or two operations, ranked by total cost. Codes are filtered by the check digit and QTY by the 1..500 range. Then search over the K-best QTY, UNIT and AMOUNT candidates for the cheapest consistent triple, using the integer constraint amount_cents == qty*unit_cents. The constraint is very selective, so two damaged fields in one row are usually still uniquely recoverable.
assumptions: Damage per value is limited to about two operations, so the candidate sets stay small (tens to hundreds)
The confusion table in the spec is the complete set of misreads
Row boundaries can be recovered beforehand by a separate layout pass
hypotheses.resources: About 60 rows × a few hundred candidates per field; using a dict keyed by amount_cents, the triple search is roughly O(|Q|·|U|), a few ms per row. Total is well under 1 s with a perf_counter guard that lowers K when time runs short.
constraints: Relies on a separate deterministic layout pass to cut rows correctly
Candidate generation must be capped to avoid blow-up on long money strings with many damaged characters
advantages: Principled handling of misreads and lost or doubled digits
Exploits the strong multiplicative constraint inside every row
Yields ranked alternatives that a later section-sum step can reuse
weaknesses: Row-local: a damaged row whose AMOUNT is consistent with a wrong QTY/UNIT pair is not caught
Layout errors pass straight through and corrupt whole rows
hypotheses.test: Remove the arithmetic constraint and choose each field's cheapest candidate on its own. If accuracy on misread and lost_chars barely changes, the joint lattice adds nothing. Also count rows where the cheapest consistent triple is wrong while the true triple is among the candidates.

hypotheses.name: Global token-stream Viterbi segmentation
hypotheses.mechanism: Dynamic programming over the flat token stream of the document body, with states (field slot within the row cycle, section context), jointly decides row segmentation, junk-line skipping and field assignment by maximizing summed token-fit and row-consistency scores.
hypotheses.principle: Tokenize the body by the inferred separator and by line breaks, keeping line breaks as soft evidence rather than hard row boundaries. The DP walks the tokens and assigns each one either to the next column slot in the cyclic column order or to junk. The transition score at a row-closing slot includes a reward when the row's best repaired values satisfy qty*unit == amount and the code passes its check digit. Wrapped rows, merged rows and inserted lines are all just alternative paths through one lattice, so layout is decided globally instead of by fragile line rules.
assumptions: The separator can be identified so the text tokenizes into field-sized pieces
Inserted junk lines contain tokens that score poorly as field values
SECTION, SUBTOTAL and TOTAL keywords are intact and act as anchors
hypotheses.resources: O(T × 4 × small) states over T ≤ ~300 tokens; each row-closing transition calls a bounded row scorer. Cache scores per token window and stay under ~200 ms.
constraints: Needs a usable tokenization: with a three-space separator, damaged spacing could merge or split tokens
Its value-level repair is only as good as the embedded row scorer
advantages: Handles wrap, merge and junk insertion uniformly and optimally instead of heuristically
Never commits early to a bad line split
Can still recover rows when a separator coincides with a wrap
weaknesses: More complex, and needs scoring weights tuned against each other
Brings little gain on documents with clean layout
A wrong junk/value decision at a token that is valid both ways can shift a whole row
hypotheses.test: On broken_layout and heavy documents, compare row-boundary accuracy against a greedy line-joining parser. If the DP does not reduce misaligned rows, which zero out all later items by position, the hypothesis fails.

hypotheses.name: Section-sum constrained beam search
hypotheses.mechanism: A beam search runs over the rows of each section, choosing among each row's top-K repaired candidates while tracking the running amount sum. Complete states are scored against candidate readings of the SUBTOTAL, and then section results are reconciled with the TOTAL and ITEMS count.
hypotheses.principle: The checksum hierarchy is used as hard redundancy: per row qty*unit = amount, per section Σamount = SUBTOTAL, and overall Σsubtotals = TOTAL with item count = ITEMS. Each row contributes a short ranked list of consistent triples. A beam keyed by (row index, running sum in cents) keeps the cheapest path per sum, and the final state must hit one of the SUBTOTAL's candidate readings. That reading may itself be damaged, so it costs channel operations. The ITEMS count also decides between split and merge hypotheses for ambiguous layout. This catches row errors that are locally consistent but globally wrong.
assumptions: Most subtotals and totals are intact or cheaply repairable, so the sum constraints are informative
The true row triple appears in each row's top-K list
Sections are small enough (≤ 60 rows total) for a beam keyed by sums to stay narrow
hypotheses.resources: Each section has ≤ 60 rows; with K ≈ 5–10 and the beam capped at a few hundred distinct sums, a section takes a few ms. Fall back to the row-local best when the perf_counter budget is exceeded.
constraints: Useless when the subtotal itself is heavily damaged and has too many readings
Depends on an upstream row-candidate generator and layout parser
advantages: Corrects locally consistent but wrong rows, e.g. a misread in AMOUNT that happens to divide cleanly
Uses ITEMS to validate the row count, guarding against position shifts
weaknesses: Sums cannot tell apart two errors that cancel, nor a code error, since codes do not enter the sums
Gives no help with code repair
Little added value on clean or lookalike documents
hypotheses.test: Count rows where the beam changes the row-local argmax, and check whether those changes are corrections or regressions against ground truth. If corrections do not clearly outnumber regressions on misread and heavy documents, the global constraint is not worth having.
